full_text_en:
Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi v. Chow Tai Fook Nominee Limited, Pacifc Gain Development Limited, and Global Lease Development Limited — Contract Dispute

[Ruling Summary]

In civil and commercial disputes involving Hong Kong and Macao, the provisions of China's conflict of laws rules for private international law and relevant theories of private international law shall be referred to, and the segmentation method shall be adopted to determine the applicable law for different issues involved. In this case, characterization and procedural matters shall be governed by the law of the forum — Mainland law. The preliminary question, involving legal inheritance and spousal property relations, shall be governed by Mainland law in accordance with the guidance of China's conflict rules. The contract dispute itself and the issue of limitation of actions shall be governed by Hong Kong law chosen by the parties in accordance with the provisions of China's conflict rules. The parties are obligated to provide to the court the Hong Kong law they have chosen to apply.

CIVIL JUDGMENT OF THE SUPREME PEOPLE'S COURT

(2015) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 9

Appellants (Plaintiffs at First Instance): Huang Yiming, male, Han Chinese, residing in Foshan City, Guangdong Province.

Agent ad litem: Dong Likun, lawyer from V&T (Shenzhen) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Mu Jianrong, lawyer from Guangdong Xingchen Law Firm.

Appellants (Plaintiffs at First Instance): Su Yuedi, female, Han Chinese, residing in Foshan City, Guangdong Province.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Shutian, lawyer from Guangdong Guangshen Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Mu Jianrong, lawyer from Guangdong Xingchen Law Firm.

Appellants (Defendants at First Instance): Chow Tai Fook Nominee Limited. Domicile: 31/F, New World Tower, 16-18 Queen's Road Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Representative: Cheng Kam Biu Wilson, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Su Bao, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wen Bin, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

Appellants (Defendants at First Instance): Pacific Gain Development Limited. Domicile: 72-76/F, Two International Finance Centre, 8 Finance Street, Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Representative: Fung Lee Woon King, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Su Bao, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wen Bin, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance): Global Lease Development Limited. Domicile: Room 1401, 14/F, New World Tower I, 18 Queen's Road Central, Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Representative: Cheng Kam Chiu Stewart, Director of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Qiu Jinyong, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Liang Songwang, lawyer from Beijing Dentons (Guangzhou) Law Firm.

The appellants Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2012) Yue Gao Fa Min Si Chu Zi No. 1 rendered by the Guangdong High People's Court on November 13, 2014, in the case of a contract dispute with the appellants Chow Tai Fook Nominee Limited (hereinafter referred to as Chow Tai Fook Company), Pacific Gain Development Limited (hereinafter referred to as Pacific Gain Company), and the respondent Global Lease Development Limited (hereinafter referred to as Global Lease Company), filed an appeal to this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing in the First Circuit Court on April 21, 2015. The agents ad litem of appellant Huang Yiming, Dong Likun, the agent ad litem of appellant Su Yuedi, Zhang Shutian, their joint agent ad litem Mu Jianrong, the joint agents ad litem of appellants Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, Su Bao and Wen Bin, and the agents ad litem of respondent Global Lease Company, Qiu Jinyong and Liang Songwang, all appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. This case has now been concluded.

Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi alleged in their complaint: In 1992, Zheng Yutong and Li Zhaoji jointly donated RMB 160 million (unless otherwise specified, amounts are in RMB) to relocate and rebuild Shunde Overseas Chinese Middle School. Later, Zheng Yutong and Li Zhaoji requested the Shunde Municipal Government to transfer the land use right of the original site of Shunde Overseas Chinese Middle School to Global Lease Company for the donated sum of RMB 160 million. In July 1993, Zheng Yutong and Li Zhaoji, on behalf of Global Lease Company, signed the "Agreement on Transfer of Land Use Right of the Original Site of Shunde Overseas Chinese Middle School" with the Shunde Municipal Planning and Land Bureau. On June 1 and June 19, 2000, Cheng Yupei, a director of Chow Tai Fook Company, and Lam Ko Yin, a director of Pacific Gain Company, as representatives of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, entered into the "Memorandum Regarding the Sale and Purchase of Shares of Global Lease Development Limited" (hereinafter referred to as the "Memorandum") and the "Share Sale Agreement" (hereinafter referred to as the "Share Sale Agreement") with Huang Guanfang (husband of Su Yuedi, father of Huang Yiming), agreeing that Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company would transfer to Huang Guanfang the shares of Global Lease Company and the rights to shareholder loans. The Memorandum stipulated the conditions precedent for the completion of the share sale, namely, Global Lease Company obtaining from the Shunde Municipal Planning and Land Bureau the state-owned land use certificate for the original site of Overseas Chinese Middle School with Global Lease Company as the user, and Global Lease Company obtaining from the relevant Shunde municipal government departments the license for real estate sale, etc. On July 30 of the same year, Cheng Yupei, again as a director and representative of Global Lease Company, signed the "Shunde State-Owned Land Use Right Grant Contract" with the Shunde Municipal Planning and Land Bureau. On September 18 and November 14, 2000, June 15, 2001, and January 2, 2002, Cheng Yupei and Lam Ko Yin, again as representatives of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, signed four supplementary agreements with Huang Guanfang, mainly concerning changes in the currency of payment, payment schedule, and interest payments. As of July 6, 2006, Huang Guanfang had paid to Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company an aggregate amount equivalent to RMB 121,652,826.60 under the contracts, as well as the RMB 20 million earnest money stipulated in the Memorandum. Subsequently, due to the inability of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company to perform their obligations under the Memorandum and the Share Sale Agreement, the contracts could not be further performed. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested the court to order the rescission of the Memorandum, the Share Sale Agreement, and all supplementary agreements signed by Huang Guanfang with Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company; and to order Chow Tai Fook Company, Pacific Gain Company, and Global Lease Company to jointly repay the principal and interest of the transfer consideration amounting to RMB 234.1 million (including the RMB 20 million earnest money under the Memorandum, the HKD 20 million and RMB 93.5 million confirmed as paid by both parties in the fourth supplementary agreement, and interest of RMB 4,861,217 arising under the agreements, totaling RMB 141,652,826.60; interest on the RMB 20 million earnest money calculated from June 19, 2000, and interest on the remaining amounts calculated from January 25, 2002, provisionally calculated to August 1, 2010), and to pay damages of HKD 45 million as stipulated in the agreement.

The court of first instance found: On June 19, 2000, Chow Tai Fook Company, Pacific Gain Company, and Huang Guanfang entered into the "Share Sale Agreement," which provided: Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company would transfer to Huang Guanfang 100% of the shares of Global Lease Company and the rights to shareholder loans; the total consideration for the transfer and shareholder loans was HKD 184.5 million. Clause 3 stipulated the payment method: (a) HKD 45 million (deposit) payable within 8 working days after signing the agreement; (b) HKD 45 million payable within 1 month after the issuance of the land use certificate; (c) the balance payable within 8 months after signing the agreement. Clause 5 provided that, in accordance with Clause 3, the transfer should be completed on or before the last day of the 8-month period after signing the agreement, or on an earlier date agreed by the parties, and the transferors should deliver to the transferee upon the completion date and after all balances have been paid in full the following documents: (i) the duly executed agreement and the deed of transfer and relevant share certificates in favour of the transferee and/or his nominee; ... (vii) the land use certificate. Clause 7 provided that, in accordance with Clause 3, upon completion of the transfer, each transferor should execute the assignment of loans, sign Annex C, and legally assign the respective shareholder loans to the transferee or his nominee. Clause 9 "Best Endeavours" provided: (a) The transferors agreed that, upon receipt of the deposit under Clause 3(a), they would use their best endeavours prior to completion to assist the transferee to take control of the land, including but not limited to issuing necessary notices to terminate tenancies and to evict occupants, trespassers, and tenants. However, at and after completion, the transferors did not guarantee that the land would be vacant upon handover. For the avoidance of doubt, the transferee acknowledged the manner in which the land was sold, and the transferors should not bear any costs or expenses incurred by the transferee in vacating the land, but the costs of issuing termination notices should be borne by the transferors. (b) The transferors agreed to guarantee that they would use their best endeavours to assist and consent to the transferee's application to establish a local company in China named Shunde Global Lease Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Shunde Global Lease Company), and appoint a person designated by the transferee as the legal representative of Shunde Global Lease Company ... The main activity and purpose of Shunde Global Lease Company was to develop the land under the "Agreement on Transfer of Land Use Right of the Original Site of Shunde Overseas Chinese Middle School." (c) From the date of issuance of the land use certificate, the transferors undertook to take all necessary measures and use their best endeavours to assist the transferee in applying to the relevant government departments or authorities for permits for the construction, building, or development of the land ... (d) The transferors undertook and agreed not to carry out any construction, building, or development on the land prior to completion. Clause 15 "Non-Compliance" provided that, without prejudice to the transferee's other rights and right to seek remedies at any time, unless otherwise agreed, if there was a material breach of the warranties, representations, and undertakings of this agreement prior to completion of the shares, or if for any reason or cause the transferors were unable to perform any of their obligations under this agreement, the transferee should be entitled to treat the transferors as having repudiated this agreement. Clause 18 "Default by Transferee" provided that, if the transferee defaulted or failed to pay the second instalment or the balance of the transfer (not attributable to the transferors' fault), and where the transferors had performed their obligations in the manner stipulated in this agreement, the transferors should be entitled to treat the transferee as having repudiated the agreement and forfeit the deposit of HKD 45 million as damages. Thereafter, neither party should make any further claim, and any excess amount (over HKD 45 million) should be refunded by the transferors to the transferee, without payment of interest. Clause 19 "Default by Transferors" provided that, except where caused by the transferee, if after the issuance of the land use certificate the transferors failed to perform their obligations under this agreement or breached the terms thereof, the transferee should be entitled to rescind this agreement, and the transferors should refund HKD 45 million and additionally pay HKD 45 million to the transferee as damages, and neither party should make any further claim. Clause 23 provided that time was of the essence of this agreement. Clause 25 "Complete Agreement" provided that this agreement constituted the entire understanding and agreement between the parties, and any representations, warranties, whether express or implied, statutory or otherwise, made by or on behalf of either party relating to or arising from the acquisition of the shares, which were not contained in or referred to in this agreement or any annex, should not give rise to any liability on the part of the party making them. Clause 27 "Governing Law and Dispute Resolution" provided that this agreement should be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, and the parties submitted to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the Hong Kong courts. The agreement was signed with the seals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, signatures of authorised persons, the signature of W.K. To & Co. and Henry W.H. Wong, the signature of Huang Guanfang, and the signature of K.C. Ho & Fong and Fong Yin Cheung.

On September 18, 2000, Chow Tai Fook Company, Pacific Gain Company, and Huang Guanfang entered into the first supplementary agreement, wherein Recital 2 provided that, in accordance with Clause 3(b) of the principal agreement and a notice from the transferors' solicitors Messrs. W.K. To & Co. to the transferee's solicitors Messrs. K.C. Ho & Fong, part of the consideration for the shares and shareholder loans of HKD 45 million (subject to further specific provisions in the principal agreement) was payable by the transferee on or before September 7, 2000. Recital 3 provided that, at the request of the transferee, the transferors had agreed to vary the payment terms for the shares and shareholder loans referred to in Clause 3(b) of the principal agreement in the following manner. Clause 1 of the variation provided that the consideration amount of HKD 45 million payable under Clause 3(b) of the principal agreement was varied to RMB 50 million, as the second installment payment, and as part of the consideration for the shares and shareholder loans: (a) On or before September 20, 2000, the transferee should pay RMB 15 million to the transferors; (b) On or before October 20, 2000, the transferee should pay RMB 15 million to the transferors; (c) On or before November 20, 2000, the transferee should pay the balance of RMB 20 million to the transferors. The agreement was signed with the seals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, signatures of authorised persons, the signature of Huang Guanfang, and the signature of K.C. Ho & Fong and Fong Yin Cheung.

On November 14, 2000, Chow Tai Fook Company, Pacific Gain Company, and Huang Guanfang entered into the second supplementary agreement, wherein Recital 2 provided that, pursuant to the "aforesaid agreements," the transferee had paid to the transferors the following amounts: (a) Deposit of HKD 45 million under Clause 3(a) of the principal agreement; (b) RMB 15 million under Clause 1(a) of the supplementary agreement; and (c) Partial payment of RMB 8 million under Clause 1(b) of the supplementary agreement (which the transferors acknowledged receipt of). Recital 3 provided that, at the request of the transferee, the transferors had agreed to vary the payment terms of the "aforesaid agreements" in the following manner. Clause 1 of the variation provided that, pursuant to Clause 1(b) of the supplementary agreement, the balance of RMB 7 million due on October 20, 2000, should be paid by the transferee to the transferors on or before November 15, 2000. Clause 2 provided that the RMB 20 million due on November 20, 2000, under Clause 1(c) of the supplementary agreement, together with interest accrued from November 21, 2000, to the date of payment at the annual rate of 6.5%, should be deferred to on or before January 20, 2001. Clause 3 provided that the balance of the total consideration of HKD 94.5 million payable on or before February 19, 2000, under Clause 3(c) of the principal agreement should be deferred to on or before May 20, 2001, including interest accrued from February 20, 2001, to the date of payment at the annual rate of 6.5%. Clause 4 provided that if the transferee failed to pay any installment due under Clauses 1, 2, or 3 above, all unpaid amounts or the balance thereof payable by the transferee under the agreements, together with the agreed interest, would immediately become due and payable on the date of default. The agreement was signed with the seals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, signatures of authorised persons, the signature of W.K. To & Co. and Henry W.H. Wong, the signature of Huang Guanfang, and the signature of K.C. Ho & Fong and Casey K.C. Ho.

On June 15, 2001, Chow Tai Fook Company, Pacific Gain Company, and Huang Guanfang entered into the third supplementary agreement, wherein Recital 2 provided that, pursuant to the "aforesaid agreements," the total amount paid by the transferee was HKD 10 million and RMB 89.3 million (which the transferors acknowledged receipt of), and the remaining purchase price of RMB 105 million became due and payable from May 20, 2001, and should be paid to the transferors. Recital 3 provided that, pursuant to the changes arising from the second supplementary agreement, the transferors were entitled to claim interest at the annual rate of 6.5%. The agreement was signed with the seals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Pacific Gain Company, signatures of authorised persons, the signature of Huang Guanfang, and the signature of K.C. Ho & Fong and Casey K.C. Ho.

On January 25, 2002, Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Huang Guanfang entered into the Fourth Supplemental Agreement, in which Clause 4 of the "Whereas" section stipulated that, notwithstanding that under the "aforesaid agreements" the Transferee had only paid part of the purchase price, the total payment being HKD 20,000,000 and RMB 93,500,000 (the Transferor hereby acknowledged receipt of such payment), the remaining balance of the purchase price was RMB 90,000,000, which became due and payable on July 21, 2001. The Transferor acknowledged that the Transferee had paid the Transferor a total of RMB 4,861,217 in interest arising under the agreements, and as of November 30, 2001, the interest on the outstanding balance of the purchase price remaining unpaid was RMB 291,609.60. Clause 5 stipulated that the Transferor, at the request of the Transferee, had agreed to further vary the payment terms under the "aforesaid agreements" in the following manner. Clause 1 of the variation terms stipulated that the Transferee hereby confirmed and verified that, as of November 30, 2001, the interest payable by the Transferee to the Transferor under the "aforesaid agreements" became due and payable on the date of signing this Agreement, totaling RMB 291,609.60 ("Accrued Interest"). To give full effect to this Agreement, the Transferee shall pay the "Accrued Interest" to the Transferor. Clause 2 stipulated that, under the "aforesaid agreements", the outstanding balance of the purchase price due and payable of RMB 90,000,000 shall be paid by the Transferee to the Transferor on or before May 31, 2002. Clause 3 stipulated that interest shall be calculated on the outstanding balance of the purchase price and unpaid interest at an annual interest rate of 6.5% from December 1, 2001 to the date of payment, which interest shall be paid on the last day of each consecutive month starting from December 2001, with the first payment to be made on December 31, 2001. Clause 4 stipulated that the transfer shall be completed immediately upon receipt of the full payment of the outstanding balance of the purchase price and the interest specified in Clause 3 above. Clause 5 stipulated that notwithstanding the terms of this Agreement and the "aforesaid agreements", the Transferor shall have the right, at any time thereafter, at its sole discretion, to declare by written notice to the Transferee that the outstanding balance of the purchase price under the "aforesaid agreements" and all accrued interest, or any part thereof, shall become due and payable, whereupon the same shall be immediately due and payable. Clause 6 stipulated that any sub-clause of any clause in this Agreement shall be deemed a sub-clause of the aforesaid agreements, and any rights and remedies set forth in this Agreement shall be deemed to be additional rights and remedies in addition to and without affecting the rights and remedies of the Transferor under the aforesaid agreements. Clause 7 stipulated that all fees and expenses, including but not limited to penalties or fees levied by mainland government authorities, incidental land development costs, and special costs specified in the principal agreement, shall be borne entirely by the Transferee. Clause 8 stipulated that all fees and expenses incidental to the negotiation, preparation and execution of this Agreement, including but not limited to the legal fees of the Transferor's legal representatives, shall be borne entirely by the Transferee. This Agreement was sealed and signed by the authorized representatives of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company, signed by Huang Guanfang, and signed by K.C. Ho & Fong, NKKAPIN of Hong Kong.

During the first instance, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi confirmed that no payments had been made to Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company after January 25, 2002.

On May 30, 2006, Hong Kong Du Weiqiang Law Firm sent a letter to Hong Kong He Junzhu and Fang Yan Law Firm, informing them that the Transferee Huang Guanfang had breached the agreement and the contract was terminated immediately. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company believed that Huang Guanfang had committed a material breach, leading to the termination of the relevant agreements on May 30, 2006. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi confirmed that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company formally terminated the performance of the equity transfer agreement on May 30, 2006, and the contract could not continue to be performed. After being notified of the termination of the contract by Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi still negotiated with Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company regarding issues related to the termination of the contract. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi believed that because Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company refused to return the funds, their rights and interests were damaged, so the cause of action for their lawsuit arose on May 30, 2006.

Further facts found: When Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi filed the lawsuit, they submitted a "Memorandum" signed on June 1, 2000, claiming that the "Memorandum" was signed by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Huang Guanfang. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company denied this. The "Memorandum" did not bear the seals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company, but had the signature of Huang Guanfang. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that the other two signatures were those of "Zheng Yupei", a director of Chow Tai Fook Company, and "Lin Gaoyan", a director of Hang Man Company, which Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company denied.

During the first instance, in the motion challenging jurisdiction filed by Chow Tai Fook Company on October 12, 2010, the motion challenging jurisdiction filed by Hang Man Company on October 29, 2010, the defense submissions filed by Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company on August 3, 2011, and the defense submissions filed by Baoyi Company on August 3, 2011 and August 26, 2011, all stated that "Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Huang Guanfang signed the 'Memorandum' on June 1, 2000". The statement of claim filed by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Baoyi Company against Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi in Hong Kong on January 3, 2012, as submitted by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, stated: "Around May to June 2000, Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Huang Guanfang drafted a 'Memorandum', but the parties did not sign the said 'Memorandum'." Clause 3.2.1 of the "Memorandum" submitted by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi stipulated: "The Buyer shall pay the Seller RMB 20,000,000 as a good faith deposit before signing the sale and purchase agreement, but the good faith deposit shall not be offset against the amount of the sale and purchase agreement. Within eight working days after signing the sale and purchase agreement, the Buyer shall pay RMB 50,000,000 into an account designated by the Seller." Clause 4 "Conditions Precedent", sub-clause 4.1, stipulated that the completion of the sale shall proceed only after the following conditions are satisfied: (1) Baoyi Company has obtained from the Land Bureau the State-owned Land Use Certificate for the plot of land with Baoyi Company as the user; (2) Baoyi Company has obtained from the relevant department of the Shunde Municipal Government the relevant license for the sale of real estate; (3) The plot of land must be vacant land, except for the attachments listed in the schedule to this Memorandum which may remain on the plot, all other temporary structures must be demolished and cleared, and all existing leases must be terminated. Clause 4.2 stipulated that the Buyer may at any time waive in writing the conditions precedent set out in Clause 4.1. Clause 17.1 stipulated that this Memorandum shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of Hong Kong.

Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi believed that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company breached the contract by failing to comply with the following contractual terms: 1. According to Clause 4.1 of the Memorandum, Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Baoyi Company were to undertake three obligations. (1) Baoyi Company to obtain the State-owned Land Use Certificate; (2) Baoyi Company to obtain the relevant license for the sale of real estate from the relevant department of the Shunde Municipal Government; (3) The plot of land must be vacant land, except for temporary structures recorded in the Memorandum, all other temporary structures must be demolished and cleared, and all existing leases must be terminated. Among these three obligations, the first obligation, obtaining the State-owned Land Use Certificate, was fulfilled in August 2000, but the second and third obligations were not fulfilled, constituting a breach of contract. 2. With respect to the four obligations under Clause 9 of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement", Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company, except for obtaining the State-owned Land Use Certificate, issuing notices to terminate leases and clearing some leases, failed to fulfill the remaining obligations, constituting a breach of contract.

Both parties confirmed that the equity transfer in this case is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Both parties submitted legal opinions to the court of first instance. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi submitted "Hong Kong Contract Law" (Volumes I and II), "Outline of Hong Kong Contract Law", and "Relevant Provisions and Explanations of Mainland Law and Hong Kong Law Applicable to This Case". The "Relevant Provisions and Explanations of Mainland Law and Hong Kong Law Applicable to This Case" stated: I. Basic Principles of Applying Hong Kong Law to This Case. According to the relevant provisions of Mainland law, Hong Kong law may be applied to this case. The Hong Kong law chosen by the parties can only be applied to resolve the contractual disputes between the parties. The law governing whether the parties can perform contractual obligations related to Mainland law is Mainland law. II. Relevant Provisions of Hong Kong Law Applicable to the Contractual Disputes in This Case. (A) Source and Authority Explanation of the Hong Kong Law Provided. Su Yuedi and Huang Yiming provided the court with two sets of three books on Hong Kong contract law, namely "Hong Kong Contract Law" (Chinese translation) (Volumes I and II) and "Outline of Hong Kong Contract Law". (B) Relevant Provisions of Hong Kong Law Applicable to the Contractual Disputes in This Case. 1. Freedom of contract and sanctity of contract are fundamental principles of the Hong Kong contract law system. Therefore, matters concerning contractual obligations and liability for breach of contract in this case shall be tried strictly in accordance with the contract. 2. Regarding liability for termination of contract due to breach, Hong Kong law and the provisions of the contract involved in this case are consistent. (1) Under Hong Kong law, parties may agree on breaches that give rise to termination of the contract, and the court will require the parties to comply with these terms. (2) Under Hong Kong law, parties may agree on the amount of damages for breach of contract, and clauses for liquidated damages are enforceable. In this case, because Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company failed to fulfill the conditions precedent stipulated in the "Memorandum" and the obligations stipulated in the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement", Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are entitled to terminate the agreement and require Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company to return all amounts already paid and pay HKD 45,000,000 in damages in accordance with Clause 19 of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement". (3) Under Hong Kong law, after the termination of the contract, interest on the amounts that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company should have returned but did not return constitutes unjust enrichment and shall be repaid to Su Yuedi and Huang Yiming. (4) Under Hong Kong law, when Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company fail to perform the contract or the contract becomes impossible to perform, Su Yuedi and Huang Yiming may refuse to perform their contractual obligations. III. Regardless of whether under Hong Kong law or Mainland law, Baoyi Company should bear the obligation to repay. 1. Under Hong Kong law and as indicated by Baoyi Company's litigation conduct, Baoyi Company is an actual party to the contracts involved in this case and is also a defendant in this case. 2. Under Hong Kong law, Su Yuedi and Huang Yiming are entitled to sue Baoyi Company to bear the obligation to repay. 3. Under Mainland law, Baoyi Company should also bear the obligation to repay. The "Certificate of Legal Opinion" submitted by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Baoyi Company stated: Xu Jiawei, a practicing barrister in Hong Kong, examined and provided Hong Kong law based on the documents and statements submitted by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hang Man Company and Baoyi Company. The conclusions of the legal opinion are as follows: I. The "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" is valid and binding on all parties. II. Huang Guanfang's failure to pay on time undermined the entire foundation of the contract and violated a "condition" of the contract terms, which was sufficient for Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company, as the non-breaching parties, to have the right to choose to terminate the contract. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company effectively terminated the contract by letter in 2006. III. After the effective termination of the contract, Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company are entitled to forfeit the amounts paid by Huang Guanfang in accordance with the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" and the four supplemental agreements, and also have the right to recover losses suffered due to his breach. IV. Baoyi Company is the target company of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement", the debtor of the shareholder loan, not the transferor or transferee, not a party to the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement", is not bound by the contract, and has no contractual rights or obligations. V. Huang Guanfang or his lawful heirs have no right to claim any contractual or shareholder loan interests from Baoyi Company. VI. He Junzhu and Fang Yanxiang Law Firm was the legal representative law firm for Huang Guanfang in signing the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement". VII. Clause 25 "Entire Agreement Clause" of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" limits the contractual relationship between the signing parties to the whole written document of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement". Any documents or promises not recorded in the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" or made prior to its execution shall not form part of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" and shall have no legal effect. VIII. Clause 26 "Assignment Clause" of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" allows lawful successors or assignees of each party to succeed to the contractual rights and be bound by the contract, provided that the consent of the other party is obtained before any party assigns contractual rights. Under Hong Kong law, "successors" refer to "executors" or "administrators" appointed by the court. Because the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" is governed by Hong Kong law, and Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have not applied under Hong Kong law to become the "executors" or "administrators" of Huang Guanfang, they are not qualified to succeed to the rights under the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement". IX. If Huang Guanfang or his purported heirs bring a lawsuit based on Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company's breach of contract as a cause of action, it must be brought within six years from the date the breach occurred. After that period, such persons cannot file a lawsuit regarding that breach. X. The transfer of equity and shareholder loans is a lawful and valid common commercial practice.

Huang Guanfang was a native of Shunde, Foshan. Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi registered their marriage on November 8, 1979, in Shunde District, Foshan City. After marriage, they had two sons, Huang Yiming and Huang Shiming. Huang Guanfang died on January 19, 2008, in Shunde District, Foshan City. According to the notarized certificates provided by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, both of Huang Guanfang's parents predeceased him. Huang Guanfang did not leave a will before his death. All statutory heirs of Huang Guanfang made declarations or dispositions regarding their inheritance rights. Su Yuedi, by a notarized declaration, stated that she renounced her inheritance of Huang Guanfang's estate. Huang Shiming, by a declaration notarized by the Consulate General of the People's Republic of China in Manchester, stated that he renounced his inheritance of Huang Guanfang's estate.

Based on the application for property preservation filed by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, the court of first instance sealed up the land use right under the name of Baoyi Company located at the former site of Huaqiao Middle School, Qinghui Road, Daliang Town, Shunde District, Foshan City, Guangdong Province, with certificate number Shunfu Guoyong (2000) Zi No. 0100878. Baoyi Company indicated that the sealed land is currently vacant and undeveloped.

The court of first instance held that: This case is a dispute over a Hong Kong-related equity transfer contract. Pursuant to the civil ruling (2011) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 32 issued by the Supreme People's Court on November 30, 2011, this court has jurisdiction over this case. Clause 17.1 of the "Memorandum" stipulated: "This Memorandum shall be governed by the laws of Hong Kong and construed in accordance with the laws of Hong Kong." Clause 27 of the "Equity Sale and Purchase Agreement" stipulated: "This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region." During the proceedings of this case, all parties confirmed that the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region should apply to this case. Article 145, paragraph 1 of the "General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China" provides: "The parties to a contract involving foreign interests may choose the law applicable to the settlement of their contractual disputes, except as otherwise provided by law." This case involves Hong Kong and shall be handled by reference to the above provision to determine the applicable law. Therefore, this case shall be governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Regarding whether Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, as plaintiffs in this case, have proper standing to sue. Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi were both natives of Shunde, Foshan. The marital relationship between Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi during his lifetime did not involve any foreign, Hong Kong, Macau or Taiwan elements. Therefore, the determination of property acquired during the subsistence of their marriage, including the property rights involved in this case, shall be governed by the "Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China". According to Article 17 of that Law, the property rights involved in this case constitute the community property of Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi. Su Yuedi, as a co-owner, is entitled to file this lawsuit regarding her property share. In the inheritance legal relationship between Huang Guanfang, Su Yuedi, Huang Yiming and Huang Shiming, there are also no foreign, Hong Kong, Macau or Taiwan elements. Therefore, the determination of whether Huang Yiming is a qualified heir shall be governed by the relevant provisions of the "Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China" and other related laws. Among the first-order statutory heirs, Su Yuedi and Huang Shiming clearly expressed their renunciation of inheritance, making Huang Yiming the sole heir of Huang Guanfang's estate. According to Article 25 of the "Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China", Huang Yiming is a proper plaintiff in this case. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company argued that the issue of qualification for inheritance in this case should be governed by Hong Kong law, and that Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi do not have proper standing as plaintiffs. This argument lacks legal basis and is not supported.

Regarding the statute of limitations issue. Both parties cited the provisions of Section 4(1)(a) of Hong Kong's "Limitation Ordinance", i.e., an action founded on contract or tort shall not be brought after the expiration of six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued. Therefore, it is confirmed that the limitation period for this case is six years from the date the cause of action accrued. The Fourth Supplemental Agreement dated January 25, 2002 stipulated that Huang Guanfang should pay the outstanding balance of RMB 90,000,000 on or before May 31, 2002, but Huang Guanfang failed to perform his payment obligation as agreed. During the proceedings of this case, the correspondence provided by Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company showed that after the final payment deadline of May 31, 2002, as stipulated in the Fourth Supplemental Agreement, Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company continued to negotiate with Huang Guanfang regarding the performance of the contract. On May 30, 2006, Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company sent a letter to Huang Guanfang clearly informing him of the termination of the equity transfer agreement. At this point, a dispute arose between the parties regarding the performance of the contract, and the cause of action for one party to request termination of the contract accrued. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi filed this lawsuit based on the termination of the relevant equity transfer agreement, the return of funds, and liability for breach of contract. The date on which the cause of action accrued should be May 30, 2006, the date on which Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company clearly informed Huang Guanfang of the termination of the equity transfer agreement. Therefore, the limitation period for this case should run from May 30, 2006. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi filed their lawsuit with the court of first instance on September 2, 2010, which did not exceed the six-year limitation period. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi argued that the date their cause of action against Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company accrued was May 30, 2006, when Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company sent the letter to Huang Guanfang terminating the contract. This argument is well-founded and is supported. The defense of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hang Man Company that the lawsuit filed by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi exceeded the six-year limitation period lacks sufficient basis and is not supported.

Regarding the determination of the breaching party. First, Huang Guanfang, Chow Tai Fook Company, and Heng Man Company successively signed the Equity Sale Agreement and four supplemental agreements for the transfer of the equity interests at issue, to which both parties have no objection and which are confirmed. Both parties, in the legal opinions submitted to the court, considered that freedom of contract and sanctity of contract are fundamental principles of the Hong Kong contract legal system, that the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements are valid and binding on both parties, and confirmed that the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements are valid, and that both parties shall perform their respective obligations in accordance with the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements. Second, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that the parties also signed a Memorandum, which Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company denied. Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, in the jurisdictional objection application and reply submitted in this case, and Baoyi Company in its reply, all expressly confirmed that "Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company signed the Memorandum with Huang Guanfang on June 1, 2000." Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company later argued that they had never signed the Memorandum, but this argument lacked a basis and is not accepted. Therefore, it is confirmed that Huang Guanfang, Chow Tai Fook Company, and Heng Man Company signed the Memorandum on June 1, 2000. Third, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company had breached the provisions of Article 4.1, paragraphs (2) and (3) of the Memorandum, thereby constituting a breach of contract. The two matters stipulated in Article 4.1, paragraphs (2) and (3) of the Memorandum, namely "Baoyi Company shall obtain the relevant licenses for real estate sales from the relevant government departments of Shunde City" and "remove and clear temporary structures and terminate leases," were amended in Article 9 of the Equity Sale Agreement. Article 9(a) of the Equity Sale Agreement stipulates, "Issue the necessary notices to terminate the lease relationships... However, upon and after the completion of the transfer, the transferor does not guarantee that the land will be vacant upon delivery of the land." Article 9(b) stipulates, "The transferor agrees to and assists the transferee in establishing Shunde Baoyi Company locally in China... The main activity and purpose of Shunde Baoyi Company is to develop the land under the Agreement for the Transfer of the Right to Use the Original Land Parcel of Overseas Chinese Middle School in Shunde City." Article 9(c) stipulates, "...use best efforts to assist the transferee in applying to the relevant government departments or authorities for permits for land construction, building, or development..." Since the parties had already amended the rights and obligations stipulated in Article 4.1, paragraphs (2) and (3) of the Memorandum, those provisions no longer bind the parties. The parties shall exercise their rights and perform their obligations in accordance with the new agreement. Therefore, the claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company violated Article 4.1, paragraphs (2) and (3) of the Memorandum and thereby constituted a breach of contract lacks a basis and is not supported. Fourth, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company violated Article 9 of the Equity Sale Agreement, thereby constituting a breach of contract. Article 9 of the Equity Sale Agreement is a "best efforts" provision, i.e., the transferor shall use best efforts to assist the transferee in obtaining control of the land, the transferor shall use its best efforts to assist and agree to the transferee establishing Shunde Baoyi Company, and the transferor shall use best efforts to assist the transferee in applying to the relevant government departments for permits for land construction, building, or development, etc. This "best efforts" clause requires Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company to use their best efforts to assist Huang Guanfang in completing the relevant matters. It is an obligation of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company to assist Huang Guanfang. In this case, there is no evidence showing that Huang Guanfang took any measures regarding establishing Shunde Baoyi Company, applying to the relevant government departments for development permits, or other related matters, nor is there evidence showing that Huang Guanfang made any request to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company for assistance in completing the relevant matters. Since Huang Guanfang did not commence the relevant matters, there was no precondition for Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company to perform the corresponding assisting obligations. Moreover, during the litigation of this case, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi confirmed that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company had issued notices to clear leases and had cleared part of the leases, and there was no evidence showing that the land at issue had been developed or constructed. Therefore, the claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company violated Article 9 of the Equity Sale Agreement and thereby constituted a breach of contract lacks a basis and is not supported. Fifth, because Huang Guanfang did not pay the equity transfer consideration as agreed in the Equity Sale Agreement, Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Huang Guanfang successively signed four supplemental agreements, agreeing to extend the payment deadline for Huang Guanfang. The fourth supplemental agreement on January 25, 2002, expressly stipulated that Huang Guanfang should pay the remaining amount of RMB 90 million by May 31, 2002, but thereafter Huang Guanfang did not make payment to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company as agreed. Therefore, Huang Guanfang's conduct constituted a breach of contract. In summary, the claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company breached the contract lacks a basis and is not supported. The defense by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that Huang Guanfang's delayed payment constituted a breach of contract is well-founded and is supported.

Regarding whether Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should return funds to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi and the amount thereof. First, pursuant to the fourth supplemental agreement on January 25, 2002, Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Huang Guanfang jointly confirmed that the amounts paid by Huang Guanfang were HKD 20 million, RMB 93.5 million, and RMB 4,861,217 in late payment interest. This payment amount is confirmed. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that they had paid RMB 20 million as earnest money to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company under the Memorandum, which Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company did not acknowledge. Since Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi failed to provide evidence proving that Huang Guanfang had paid RMB 20 million as earnest money to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, that claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi is not supported. Second, Article 18 of the Equity Sale Agreement, "Default by Transferee," stipulates, "If the transferee defaults or fails to pay the second installment or the remaining balance of the equity transfer (not attributable to the transferor), and when the transferor has performed its obligations in the manner provided in this agreement, the transferor shall have the right to deem the transferee as rejecting the agreement and to forfeit the deposit of HKD 45 million as liquidated damages. Thereafter, neither party shall make any further claims, and any excess amount (above HKD 45 million) shall be returned by the transferor to the transferee without interest." Because Huang Guanfang's failure to pay the remaining equity transfer consideration as agreed constituted a breach of contract, on May 30, 2006, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company sent a letter to Huang Guanfang clearly informing him of the termination of the equity transfer agreement. During the litigation of this case, both parties confirmed that the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements had been rescinded on May 30, 2006. Therefore, it is confirmed that the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements are rescinded. Since the Memorandum and the Equity Sale Agreement were contracts signed regarding the same equity transfer matter, and under the circumstance where both parties confirmed the rescission of the Equity Sale Agreement and the four supplemental agreements, the claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi to rescind the Memorandum is well-founded and is supported. After the rescission of the contracts, in accordance with Article 18 of the Equity Sale Agreement, Huang Guanfang had paid HKD 20 million and RMB 98,361,217 to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company. After deducting HKD 45 million, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company shall return the remaining amount to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi. Since Article 18 of the Equity Sale Agreement expressly stipulates that neither party shall make any further claims and that the returned funds do not bear interest, the claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi for interest lacks a basis and is not supported. In summary, the amount to be returned by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi is RMB 98,361,217 minus HKD 25 million (deducted after conversion into RMB based on the central parity rate of RMB against HKD published by the People's Bank of China on May 30, 2006).

Regarding whether Baoyi Company should bear the repayment obligation. This case is a dispute over an equity transfer contract. Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company signed the Equity Sale Agreement with Huang Guanfang, agreeing to transfer to Huang Guanfang 100% of the equity in Baoyi Company and the loan rights of the shareholders. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claimed that Baoyi Company should jointly bear the repayment obligation with Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company. Baoyi Company is merely the target company of the shares transferred under the Equity Sale Agreement; it is not a party to the contract, nor is it the transferor or transferee of the shareholder loan rights. It is a third party outside the contract and therefore is not bound by the contract. The claim by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Baoyi Company should jointly bear the repayment obligation with Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company lacks a basis and is not supported.

In summary, some of the claims by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are well-founded and are supported; the other claims lack a basis and are dismissed. In accordance with Article 145, paragraph 1 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 17 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 25 of the Succession Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 64 and 69 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court hereby renders the following judgment: 1. It is confirmed that the Memorandum signed by Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Huang Guanfang on June 1, 2000, is rescinded; the Equity Sale Agreement signed by Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Huang Guanfang on June 19, 2000, the First Supplemental Agreement signed on September 18, 2000, the Second Supplemental Agreement signed on November 14, 2000, the Third Supplemental Agreement signed on June 15, 2001, and the Fourth Supplemental Agreement signed on January 25, 2002, are rescinded. 2. Within thirty days from the date this judgment becomes legally effective, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company shall return to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi the following amount: RMB 98,361,217 minus HKD 25 million (deducted after conversion into RMB based on the central parity rate of RMB against HKD published by the People's Bank of China on May 30, 2006). 3. All other claims of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are dismissed. If the obligation to pay money is not fulfilled within the period specified in the judgment, interest on the debt for the period of delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 253 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. The first-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 1,212,255.50, of which Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi shall bear RMB 812,255.50, and Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company shall bear RMB 400,000.

Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, dissatisfied with the above first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court, stating:

(I) The first-instance judgment erred in characterizing the nature of this case solely as a dispute over equity transfer. The dispute in this case involves not only equity transfer but also the transfer of shareholder loan rights. 1. According to Article 3.1 and Article 3.2 of the Memorandum and the "Whereas" clause, Articles 2, 3, and 4 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, the subject matter of the contract transfer includes not only equity but also the shareholder's loan claims against the company. 2. In their jurisdictional objection applications to the first-instance court and their pleadings to the Supreme People's Court, Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company all confirmed that this case is a dispute over equity transfer and debt assignment. 3. In both its jurisdictional ruling and the findings of fact in its first-instance judgment, the first-instance court confirmed that this case involves both equity transfer and debt assignment. 4. The Supreme People's Court's ruling already pointed out that "the contracts involved in this case, though named equity transfer contracts, also involve the assignment of creditor's rights."

(II) The first-instance judgment erred in determining that Baoyi Company should not bear joint repayment liability. Under Hong Kong law and Mainland law, Baoyi Company, as the debtor in this case, should bear joint repayment liability together with Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company. 1. Pursuant to Section 9 of the Law Amendment and Reform (Consolidation) Ordinance of Hong Kong, when a party assigns a creditor's right by written contract, the assignee is entitled to all legal rights of the assignor against the debtor, including rights of action and relief. If the debtor becomes aware of a dispute between the assignor and assignee concerning the assignment of the creditor's right, and the debtor wishes to discharge the debt, the debtor should pay the amount into court. 2. The Supreme People's Court's ruling explicitly identified Baoyi Company as the debtor in this case. Under Hong Kong law, since Baoyi Company is the debtor in the dispute over the assignment of creditor's rights in this case, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have the right to demand that Baoyi Company assume joint repayment liability. 3. The adversarial lawsuit filed by Baoyi Company against Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi in Hong Kong, as well as the evidence submitted by Baoyi Company, all indicate that Baoyi Company is the debtor in this case and should bear the repayment obligation according to law. On March 24, 2011, Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company, as the first, second, and third plaintiffs respectively, filed a lawsuit against Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi in the High Court of Hong Kong, case number HCA499/2011, seeking judgments: (1) confirming that the Equity Purchase Agreement and the Supplemental Agreement are governed by Hong Kong law and are valid; (2) confirming that Huang Guanfang breached the contract and that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company have lawfully terminated the Equity Purchase Agreement; (3) ordering Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi to pay damages to Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company, and confirming that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company are entitled to and have lawfully forfeited all payments made by Huang Guanfang under the Equity Purchase Agreement and the Supplemental Agreement; (4) granting an injunction prohibiting Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi from commencing and/or continuing any legal proceedings against the three plaintiffs in China or any other jurisdiction regarding the above matters, particularly the Equity Purchase Agreement as supplemented, including but not limited to the Guangdong litigation; (5) ordering interest, costs, and other relief as the court deems appropriate. The High Court of Hong Kong accepted the case. On January 4, 2012, Baoyi Company submitted an application to the High Court of Hong Kong to amend its claims, requesting judgment: confirming that Huang Guanfang breached the contract and that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company have lawfully terminated the Equity Purchase Agreement and the Supplemental Agreement. Clearly, Baoyi Company made the request to the Hong Kong court as a contracting party. 4. Under Hong Kong agency law, Baoyi Company should be bound by the Memorandum and the Equity Purchase Agreement. Baoyi Company's Articles of Association provide that the company's directors are responsible for its operations and represent the company in handling major matters. Cheng Yu-tung and Lee Shau-kee, who represented Baoyi Company in signing the Land Use Rights Transfer Agreement with the Shunde Municipal Government, and Cheng Yu-pei, who represented Baoyi Company in signing the Land Use Rights Grant Contract with the Shunde Municipal Government, were all representatives who signed the Memorandum and the Equity Purchase Agreement with Huang Guanfang. Thus, the Memorandum, the Equity Purchase Agreement, and their Supplemental Agreements were all signed by the directors of Baoyi Company, and the number of directors signing these documents exceeded 50% of Baoyi Company's board membership. The directors of Baoyi Company are its agents; therefore, Baoyi Company should be bound by the contract terms. 5. Pursuant to Articles 73 and 80 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are entitled to demand that Baoyi Company, together with Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company, assume joint repayment liability after the contract's rescission. 6. The obligations under Article 4.2 of the Memorandum and Article 9 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, such as "obtaining the state-owned land use certificate and real estate sales license, clearing temporary structures and leases on the land," "terminating lease relationships, evicting occupants, illegal possessors, and lessees," establishing Shunde Baoyi Company, and applying for relevant permits, could only be performed by Baoyi Company. This shows that Baoyi Company is bound by the contract terms. 7. A letter from Baoyi Company to a third party, Mr. Lu Kangming, indicates that Baoyi Company acknowledged signing the Memorandum involved in this case.

(III) The first-instance judgment erred in finding that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company did not breach the contract. Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company failed to fulfill the conditions precedent stipulated in the Memorandum and also failed to fully perform their obligations under the Equity Purchase Agreement, resulting in the failure to achieve the purpose of the contract. They should bear liability for breach of contract. Huang Guanfang's exercise of the right of defense to stop payment should not be deemed as a breach. 1. The Memorandum and the Equity Purchase Agreement independently stipulate the contractual obligations of Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company, and there is no substitution relationship between them. The conditions precedent in the Memorandum were not altered by Article 9 of the Equity Purchase Agreement or by any other provisions. 2. As per Article 4 of the Memorandum, the transaction could only proceed after Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company fulfilled three obligations: obtaining the state-owned land use certificate, obtaining the real estate sales license, and clearing and demolishing all temporary buildings on the land and terminating all existing leases. These three obligations were to be completed within eight months from the date of signing the Memorandum; otherwise, liability for breach of contract would arise. However, aside from obtaining the state-owned land use certificate, the other two obligations were never fulfilled by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company. Their actions prevented the satisfaction of the contract's conditions precedent, making it impossible to proceed with the transfer of equity and shareholder loan rights, the basic content of which was the transfer of the land use rights of the former Overseas Chinese Middle School in Shunde City. 3. According to Article 32 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, headings in the contract cannot be used for conclusive interpretation of relevant clauses. Therefore, the actions under Article 9, such as terminating lease relationships, establishing Shunde Baoyi Company, and obtaining land title certificates, are actions that only Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company could perform, and these were their contractual obligations. At that time, Huang Guanfang had not yet obtained shareholder status in Baoyi Company and was fundamentally unable to handle the above matters. 4. According to the contract terms and Hong Kong law, when Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company breach the contract, Huang Guanfang has the right to exercise the right of defense, the right to rescind the contract, and the right to request the return of payments and compensation for damages. 5. On December 7, 2012, in the absence of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, the High Court of Hong Kong rendered a ruling under Hong Kong law, dismissing the applications by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company seeking confirmation that Huang Guanfang breached the contract and that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company had lawfully terminated the Equity Purchase Agreement and the Supplemental Agreement. Thus, the High Court of Hong Kong, applying Hong Kong law, determined that Huang Guanfang did not breach the contract.

(IV) The first-instance court, while confirming the validity of the Memorandum, denied that Huang Guanfang paid the RMB 20 million earnest money solely on the ground of the absence of payment vouchers. This violates both the contract terms and the principle of preponderance of evidence in civil litigation. Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company should repay the RMB 20 million earnest money paid by Huang Guanfang under the Memorandum. 1. The Memorandum stipulated that the payment of the RMB 20 million earnest money was a condition precedent for signing the Equity Purchase Agreement. The signing of the Equity Purchase Agreement proves that Huang Guanfang had already paid this amount. 2. The amount of the transfer consideration stipulated in both the Memorandum and the Equity Purchase Agreement also proves that Huang Guanfang had paid this amount.

(V) The first-instance judgment, in finding the contract rescinded and ordering Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company to bear repayment liability but without ordering interest, misinterpreted the contract terms and violated legal provisions. Under Hong Kong law, after contract rescission, interest on amounts that should be returned but have not been returned constitutes unjust enrichment. Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company should bear interest on the unreturned amounts from the date of contract rescission. Article 18 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, which states "no interest payable," refers to interest on amounts paid before the rescission does not need to be paid; it does not include interest on the delayed repayment after rescission. In summary, they request the reversal of the first-instance judgment and a judgment in favor of all their claims.

Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company responded:

(I) During the performance of the Equity Purchase Agreement, Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company were the compliant parties and did not engage in any breach of contract. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company never signed the Memorandum with Huang Guanfang, so Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's reliance on the "conditions precedent" in the Memorandum to allege breach by Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company is unfounded. Even if the Memorandum existed, according to Article 25 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, neither party may rely on documents, correspondence, discussions, or dialogues that occurred before the contract's signing or during negotiations to contradict any written content of the contract. Therefore, the Memorandum, formed before the signing of the Equity Purchase Agreement, effectively no longer has any legal effect. The obligation in Article 9 of the Equity Purchase Agreement is merely an ancillary obligation of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company to assist Huang Guanfang, and its performance is conditional on Huang Guanfang first taking proactive measures on relevant matters and requesting assistance from Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company to help complete such matters. In this case, there is no evidence that Huang Guanfang took such actions.

(II) According to the Equity Purchase Agreement and the four Supplemental Agreements, it is clear that Huang Guanfang refused to fulfill his payment obligations as agreed. Although Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company granted multiple extensions to Huang Guanfang for the payment of the equity transfer consideration, Huang Guanfang never paid the equity transfer consideration and overdue interest within the stipulated time and amount, constituting a fundamental breach. As the breaching party, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have no right to exercise the right of defense against the compliant Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company.

(III) Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's claims for return of payments and damages are all based on the premise that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company breached the contract. Therefore, their claims should be dismissed according to law.

(IV) The Memorandum is not genuine or valid, and Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have no evidence to prove that Huang Guanfang paid the RMB 20 million earnest money. Therefore, their claim for the return of the RMB 20 million earnest money should be dismissed.

(V) The Equity Purchase Agreement and the four Supplemental Agreements were lawfully rescinded due to Huang Guanfang's breach. According to the contract terms and Hong Kong law, Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company are entitled to forfeit all equity transfer payments (including the deposit of HKD 45 million) made by Huang Guanfang and are not required to return any amount to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi.

Baoyi Company responded:

(I) Huang Guanfang failed to acquire the equity of Baoyi Company and the shareholder loan rights pursuant to the Equity Purchase Agreement and the four Supplemental Agreements. Therefore, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have no right to assert any claims against Baoyi Company.

(II) Baoyi Company is merely the debtor of the shareholder loans of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company, not the debtor of Huang Guanfang. Consequently, it cannot be determined that Baoyi Company is liable to repay Huang Guanfang.

(III) This case is a dispute arising from the performance of the Equity Purchase Agreement between Huang Yiming, Su Yuedi, and Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company. The signing and performance of the contract occurred in Hong Kong. The Mainland court originally had no jurisdiction over this case. However, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi named Baoyi Company, which is unrelated to this case, as a defendant, thereby abusing their litigation rights to obtain jurisdiction from the Mainland court. The outcome of this trial shows that Baoyi Company is not liable. During the performance of the contract before his death, due to insufficient funds, Huang Guanfang requested an extension of the payment deadline and entered into multiple Supplemental Agreements with Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company. Yet Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi claim that Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company breached the contract and seek claims exceeding RMB 200 million, seeking illegal benefits. Their claims should not be supported.

Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company, also dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court, stating:

(I) The first-instance court's confirmation that Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Huang Guanfang signed the Memorandum is inconsistent with the objective facts. The authenticity of the Memorandum submitted by Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi cannot be established. 1. The English signature of "Cheng Yu-pei" on the Memorandum was maliciously forged. 2. Lin Gaoyan submitted a written declaration to the court during the first instance, denying having signed the Memorandum. Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company also applied to the first-instance court for a forensic handwriting examination of the Memorandum, but the application was not granted. 3. The jurisdictional objection applications and pleadings submitted by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company during the jurisdictional objection phase were only temporary references to the content stated in Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's complaint for the purpose of resolving the procedural issue of jurisdiction, and do not constitute acknowledgment of the authenticity of the Memorandum. 4. In the Hong Kong litigation, the complaint filed by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company stated: "Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Huang Guanfang drafted the Memorandum, but the parties did not sign the said Memorandum."

(II) Given that Huang Guanfang's breach of contract has already been confirmed, the claims of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, which are based on the alleged breach by Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company, should be dismissed. The second holding of the first-instance judgment seriously violates the basic principle of "no trial without complaint" in civil litigation. Whether and how to pursue legal liability arising from Huang Guanfang's breach should be handled in a separate case; this is the right of Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company.

(III) The first-instance court erred in its findings of fact. 1. The interest of RMB 4,861,217 confirmed in the Fourth Supplemental Agreement was additional liability voluntarily assumed by Huang Guanfang to Chow Tai Fook Company and Hangmen Company due to his failure to pay the transfer price on time; it was not part of the principal of the transfer price. 2. Under Hong Kong law, the limitation period for this case is six years from the date the cause of action arose. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi explicitly stated that the contract was rescinded on May 31, 2002, and they seek to hold Chow Tai Fook Company, Hangmen Company, and Baoyi Company liable from that date. Therefore, the date on which their cause of action arose should be May 31, 2002. Accordingly, this case has clearly exceeded the six-year limitation period. 3. This case is governed by Hong Kong law. After Huang Guanfang's death, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi failed to provide evidence that they had fulfilled the legal formalities under Hong Kong law to become Huang Guanfang's executors or administrators. Therefore, they lack the standing to bring this action.

(IV) The Supreme People's Court's ruling held that although the contracts involved in this case are named equity transfer contracts, they also involve the transfer of shareholder loan rights. As the debtor, Baoyi Company has a legal interest in this case. Since the defendant Baoyi Company has seizable property within Guangdong Province, the first-instance court has jurisdiction over this case. However, that ruling granted the first-instance court only provisional jurisdiction. Based on the facts found in the first instance, Baoyi Company is not required to bear any liability, and the factual basis for the provisional jurisdiction has ceased to exist. Pursuant to Article 265 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 27 of the Equity Purchase Agreement, this case should be under the jurisdiction of the Hong Kong court. Additionally, under the "forum non conveniens" principle established in Article 532 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's complaint should be dismissed. In summary, they request that the first-instance judgment be amended, that the part of the first holding concerning the rescission of the Memorandum be deleted, that the second holding be reversed, and that the other claims of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi be dismissed.

Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi argued in their defense: (1) Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company entered into and partially performed the Memorandum, and the terms of the Memorandum were not amended by the Share Purchase Agreement. This case is not merely a dispute over equity transfer but also a dispute over debt assignment. The court of first instance erred in characterizing this case solely as a dispute over equity transfer and consequently erred in determining that Bao Yi Company, as the target company of the equity transfer, should not bear liability for repayment. These findings are clearly erroneous. The execution of the Share Purchase Agreement proves that Huang Guanfang had paid the earnest money as stipulated in Clause 3.2.1 of the Memorandum. The total contract price stipulated in the Share Purchase Agreement was calculated by deducting RMB 20 million from the total price set forth in the Memorandum. The judgment of the first instance, which ignored these facts and failed to find that Huang Guanfang had paid the RMB 20 million earnest money, was erroneous. (2) The evidence provided by Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company proves that they not only breached the Memorandum but also breached the Share Purchase Agreement. On July 25, 2003, Huang Guanfang requested that Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company provide receipts for the full payment of RMB 160 million for the land transfer fee and provide the "construction approval and government approval procedures" for the original site of Shunde Overseas Chinese High School to facilitate the completion of the transaction, but they have yet to fulfill this obligation. (3) Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company did not file a counterclaim on issues such as whether Huang Guanfang had breached the contract, whether he should bear liability for breach, or whether compensation should be deducted. Therefore, the first-instance judgment's finding that Huang Guanfang breached the contract and should bear liability for breach violated the principle of "no trial without complaint." (4) This case is not time-barred. Article 4(1)(a) of the Hong Kong Limitation Ordinance provides that an action founded on a simple contract or tort shall not be brought after the expiration of six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued. This contract falls under such category, and the limitation period should be six years from the date the cause of action accrued. During the performance period after the execution of the Memorandum, the Share Purchase Agreement, and the supplementary agreements, the dispute between the parties regarding the termination of the contract and the return of payments only began on May 30, 2006, when Chow Tai Fook Company and others sent a letter to Huang Guanfang notifying him of the termination of the agreement. Therefore, the date on which the cause of action for Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's claims regarding the termination of the contract, return of payments, and liability for breach accrued should be May 30, 2006. After negotiations failed, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi filed this lawsuit in July 2010; therefore, it is within the six-year limitation period. (5) Under mainland law, Huang Yiming is the heir to Huang Guanfang's estate, and Su Yuedi is Huang Guanfang's wife. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi have the standing to bring this lawsuit, and Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company have already acknowledged the standing of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi through their own litigation conduct. Therefore, the appeals of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should be dismissed.

This court found in the second instance: Clause 14 of the Share Purchase Agreement, concerning "Representations and Warranties," stipulates that the transferor makes the following representations to the transferee: (f)(x) Except for entering into the Chinese agreement and the land lease agreement, Bao Yi Company has not and will not engage in business operations or take actions that give rise to contingent liabilities, except as already disclosed (including but not limited to construction, building, and land development). Clause 32, concerning "Headings," stipulates that any heading or subheading in this agreement is for reference only and shall not be used for conclusive interpretation of the relevant provisions.

During the second instance, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company applied for a judicial forensic examination of the authenticity of the signatures of "Cheng Yupei" and "Lin Gaoyan" on the Memorandum. Although Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company denied the authenticity of the Memorandum, in their statement of claim filed in Hong Kong, Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company stated that "around May to June 2000, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company (jointly as sellers) and Huang Guanfang (as buyer) negotiated regarding the sale and purchase of the shares of Bao Yi Company. During the negotiation, a document entitled 'Memorandum' was drafted." They also mentioned that "although the sellers and buyer did not sign the aforesaid Memorandum, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company (jointly as sellers) and Huang Guanfang (as buyer) subsequently signed the 'Share Purchase Agreement' on June 19, 2000," and they submitted the Memorandum as evidence favorable to them to the Court of First Instance of the High Court of Hong Kong.
