It is thus evident that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company do not deny the authenticity of the Memorandum itself; they only argue that it was not formally signed. Therefore, the first-instance court's confirmation of the authenticity of the Memorandum was correct. Consequently, there is no need to conduct a judicial forensic examination of the authenticity of the signatures of "Cheng Yupei" and "Lin Gaoyan" on the Memorandum. The application for forensic examination by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company is rejected.

The parties have no objection to the other facts found by the first-instance judgment and did not submit new evidence during the second instance. Therefore, except for the supplementation of part of the contract terms as set forth above, this court confirms the facts found in the first-instance judgment.

This court holds:

(1) Regarding the nature of the case. Pursuant to Article 19 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations (I) and Article 8 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations, the characterization of the dispute in this case shall be governed by the law of the forum—mainland law. Examining the content of the disputed contracts in this case, they involve the transfer of two types of rights and interests: first, the transfer by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company of all their shares in Bao Yi Company to Huang Guanfang, and second, the transfer by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company of their shareholder loan rights against Bao Yi Company to Huang Guanfang. Therefore, this case is essentially a dispute over a contract for the transfer of equity and debt. According to the requirements of the Supreme People's Court's Notice on Issuing the Revised Provisions on the Causes of Action for Civil Cases (Fa [2011] No. 42) and the attached Provisions on the Causes of Action for Civil Cases, if no provision exists at the third-level cause of action, the corresponding second-level cause of action shall apply. The cause of action in this case should be determined as a contract dispute. The first-instance court's characterization of this case solely as a dispute over equity transfer was inappropriate and should be corrected. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's position that this case involves not only an equity transfer but also a debt transfer is correct, but the cause of action should still be determined as a contract dispute.

(2) Whether Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are proper plaintiffs in this case. The issue of whether the plaintiff is a proper party is primarily a procedural matter. Procedural matters should be governed by the law of the forum—mainland law. Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A plaintiff must be a citizen, legal person, or any other organization that has a direct interest in the case." Are Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi citizens who have a direct interest in this case? This is a preliminary question in this case. Article 12 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations (I) provides: "Where the resolution of a foreign-related civil dispute must be premised on the determination of another foreign-related civil relationship, the people's court shall determine the applicable law according to the nature of that preliminary question." In this case, Huang Yiming asserts his rights and interests as the statutory heir of Huang Guanfang, and Su Yuedi asserts her rights and interests as the co-owner of the marital property with Huang Guanfang. Article 31 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations provides: "Statutory succession shall be governed by the law of the decedent's habitual residence at the time of death, except that statutory succession of immovable property shall be governed by the law of the place where the immovable property is located." The habitual residence of the decedent, Huang Guanfang, at the time of his death was in the mainland. Therefore, the first-instance court's application of mainland law and, pursuant to Article 25(1) of the Inheritance Law of the People's Republic of China, its determination that Huang Yiming is the lawful heir of Huang Guanfang and is entitled to inherit the property involved in this case, was correct. Article 24 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations provides: "With respect to matrimonial property relations, the parties may agree to choose the law of the habitual residence of either party, the law of the nationality of either party, or the law of the principal place of the property. If the parties have not made a choice, the law of their common habitual residence shall apply; if they have no common habitual residence, the law of their common nationality shall apply." The common habitual residence of Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi was in the mainland. Therefore, the first-instance court's application of mainland law and, pursuant to Article 17 of the Marriage Law of the People's Republic of China, its determination that the property involved in this case constitutes the marital property of Huang Guanfang and Su Yuedi and that Su Yuedi is the co-owner of the disputed property, was correct. After Huang Guanfang's death, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, as his heir and co-owner of the property respectively, filed this lawsuit, which clearly meets the requirement of "plaintiff" under Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China. They are the proper plaintiffs in this case. The argument of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that Hong Kong law should apply to determine whether Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are proper parties to this lawsuit is erroneous.

(3) Regarding the jurisdiction of this case. This court's civil ruling (2011) Min Si Zhong Zi No. 32 has already determined that the mainland court has jurisdiction over this case. The parties are no longer entitled to raise objections to jurisdiction. Furthermore, according to the principle of jurisdictional constancy, even if the facts on which jurisdiction was based change during the course of the proceedings, it does not affect the jurisdiction of the court that was established at the time the plaintiff filed the lawsuit and the court accepted it, so as to maintain the values of procedural stability and litigation efficiency. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi named Bao Yi Company as a defendant in this case. Whether Bao Yi Company should bear liability is a matter that can only be finally determined after substantive trial. Therefore, the argument of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that, based on reasons such as so-called provisional jurisdiction and the doctrine of forum non conveniens, the lawsuit of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi should be dismissed, is untenable.

(4) Regarding the assumption of liability for breach of contract under the contracts involved in this case. This case is a contract dispute involving Hong Kong. Clause 17 of the Memorandum stipulates: "This Memorandum shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of Hong Kong." Clause 27 of the Share Purchase Agreement stipulates: "This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region." The first-instance court's application of Article 145(1) of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China to determine that the contract dispute in this case should be governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region was correct. The parties have no objection to this point. Examining the contracts from the perspectives of form, the contracting capacity of the parties, expression of intent, consideration, and purpose, the Memorandum, the Share Purchase Agreement, and the four supplementary agreements all meet the conditions for validity under Hong Kong contract law. The first-instance court's finding that the Memorandum, the Share Purchase Agreement, and the four supplementary agreements are all valid is correct. Both parties have expressed their intention to terminate the contracts. The Memorandum, the Share Purchase Agreement, and the four supplementary agreements should be terminated.

Clause 25 of the Share Purchase Agreement stipulates: "This Agreement contains the entire understanding and agreement of the parties, and no representations or warranties, whether express or implied, statutory or otherwise, relating to or arising from the acquisition of the shares, made by or on behalf of a party, which are not contained or referred to in this Agreement or any schedule hereto, shall give rise to any liability on the part of the person making such representations or warranties." Pursuant to this clause, a breach of the Memorandum does not give rise to legal liability. In this sense, the Share Purchase Agreement has effectively superseded the Memorandum. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's claim to pursue liability for breach against Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company based on Clause 4 of the Memorandum lacks a legal basis. Pursuant to the Share Purchase Agreement, the primary contractual obligations of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company were to transfer all shares in Bao Yi Company and the shareholder loan rights against Bao Yi Company to Huang Guanfang upon full payment of the transfer price. Huang Guanfang's primary contractual obligation was to pay the price of HKD 184.5 million. Clause 9 of the Share Purchase Agreement relates to ancillary obligations of the transferors, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company. In this case, Huang Guanfang failed to complete the payment within the period stipulated in the Share Purchase Agreement. Even after entering into four supplementary agreements and extending the payment deadline, he still failed to complete payment. The Share Purchase Agreement does not expressly provide that payment of the transfer price is conditional upon Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company performing specific obligations. Therefore, the first-instance court's finding that Huang Guanfang breached the contract and its rejection of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's claim seeking a finding that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company breached the contract were not improper. The grounds of appeal of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should bear liability for breach and that Huang Guanfang's suspension of payment constituted the exercise of a right of defense and did not constitute a breach, are untenable.

Clause 18 of the Share Purchase Agreement stipulates that in the event of default by the transferee, the transferor is entitled to "forfeit the deposit of HKD 45 million as liquidated damages," and "thereafter, neither party shall make any further claims, and any surplus funds shall be refunded by the transferor to the transferee without interest." Pursuant to this clause, in the event of Huang Guanfang's default, Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company are only entitled to retain HKD 45 million; the remaining amounts shall be refunded, and no further claims may be made. Huang Guanfang had paid HKD 20 million, RMB 93.5 million, and RMB 4,861,217. After deducting HKD 45 million from these amounts, the first-instance court's judgment ordering Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company to return to Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi "RMB 98,361,217 minus HKD 25 million" was correct. Although the RMB 4,861,217 paid by Huang Guanfang was initially intended as interest, since Huang Guanfang's liability for breach is limited to HKD 45 million, all payments made by him, regardless of their nature, should be included in the total amount paid and refunded by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company after deducting HKD 45 million. The ground of appeal of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that the RMB 4,861,217 should not be refunded is untenable. At the same time, Clause 18 of the Share Purchase Agreement expressly provides that the refund of the surplus by the transferor to the transferee shall be without interest. Therefore, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi are not entitled to claim interest on this amount. Their argument that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should pay interest on the refunded amount is a misinterpretation of the contract terms, and this ground of appeal is untenable.

Based on the facts found, the court's determination, after finding Huang Guanfang in breach, of the legal liability each party should bear upon termination of the contract is an inherent part of resolving the contract dispute. While the first-instance judgment dismissed the claims of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi based on the alleged breach by Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, it was correct for it to also address in the same proceeding the amounts that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should refund under the contract. This did not exceed the scope of trial and does not violate the fundamental litigation principle of "no trial without complaint." The ground of appeal of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that the legal liability arising from Huang Guanfang's breach should be dealt with in a separate proceeding is untenable.

(5) Whether the RMB 20 million earnest money under the Memorandum has been paid. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi argue that Huang Guanfang paid the RMB 20 million earnest money pursuant to the Memorandum. Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company deny this. Under these circumstances, Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi did not provide sufficient evidence to prove that Huang Guanfang actually paid this amount to Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company. Their argument is merely an inference based on the provision regarding earnest money in the Memorandum and the determination of the price in the Share Purchase Agreement, which cannot meet the standard of proof of high probability and cannot lead the judge to form a convinced belief. Therefore, the first-instance court's failure to find that Huang Guanfang paid the RMB 20 million earnest money was not improper. The ground of appeal of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company should refund the RMB 20 million earnest money lacks factual basis and is untenable.

(6) Whether Bao Yi Company should assume the debts in this case. Bao Yi Company was not a party to the Memorandum, the Share Purchase Agreement, or the four supplementary agreements. It was merely the target company under the equity transfer and the debtor under the debt assignment as stipulated in the contracts. Pursuant to Article 9 of the Hong Kong Law Amendment and Reform (Consolidation) Ordinance, it cannot be concluded that Bao Yi Company is liable to pay Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi in this case. The first-instance court's rejection of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi's claim that Bao Yi Company should bear repayment liability was correct. The ground of appeal of Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi that, under both Hong Kong law and mainland law, Bao Yi Company should jointly bear the repayment liability with Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, is untenable.

(7) Regarding the limitation of action in this case. Article 7 of the Law of the People's Republic of China on Choice of Law for Foreign-Related Civil Relations provides: "Limitation of actions shall be governed by the law applicable to the related foreign-related civil relationship." The limitation of action in this case should therefore be determined by the law applicable to the contract dispute—the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region. Article 4(1)(a) of the Hong Kong Limitation Ordinance provides that an action founded on contract or tort shall not be brought after the expiration of six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued. The first-instance court's application of this provision to find that the limitation period for this case is six years was correct. The parties have no objection to this, but they disagree on the starting point of the limitation period. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi argue that it should start from May 30, 2006, while Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company argue that it should start from May 31, 2002. Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi filed this lawsuit based on the contracts entered into between Huang Guanfang and Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, seeking confirmation of the termination of the contracts and requesting Chow Tai Fook Company, Heng Man Company, and Bao Yi Company to return the paid transfer price and interest and to compensate for losses. Although the contract stipulated that the deadline for Huang Guanfang's payment was May 31, 2002, the date on which Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company notified Huang Guanfang of the termination of the contract was May 30, 2006. Thereafter, the parties continued to negotiate related issues after the termination. Only when they failed to reach an agreement did Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi file this lawsuit. It is thus evident that the cause of action in this case accrued on May 30, 2006, not May 31, 2002. Therefore, the first-instance judgment's finding that this case is not time-barred is correct. The ground of appeal of Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company that this case is time-barred is untenable.

In summary, the first-instance court's finding of basic facts was clear and the application of law was correct, and the judgment should be affirmed. The grounds of appeal of the appellants Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi, and of the appellants Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company, are all untenable and should not be supported. Pursuant to subparagraph (1) of Article 170(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, this court hereby orders as follows:

Appeals dismissed, and the original judgment affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 1,212,255.50, to be borne by the appellants Huang Yiming and Su Yuedi in the amount of RMB 606,127.75, and by the appellants Chow Tai Fook Company and Heng Man Company in the amount of RMB 606,127.75.

This judgment is final.
